scenarios.title: Whose patch is it?
scenarios.situation: A VM running in a public cloud IaaS account is breached through an unpatched operating system. The customer argues the cloud provider should have patched it.
scenarios.prompt: Who is responsible for patching the guest OS under the shared-responsibility model?
choices: The customer — in IaaS the provider secures the physical layer and hypervisor; the guest OS is yours
The cloud provider — they own everything below your data
Nobody — shared means neither side
The OS vendor, automatically
scenarios.why: Shared responsibility splits at the hypervisor for IaaS: the provider secures facilities, hardware, and virtualization; you own the OS, middleware, apps, and data. The line moves up the stack with PaaS and SaaS, but IaaS guests are always the customer's job.
scenarios.hint: In IaaS, where does the provider's job end?

scenarios.title: The spiky web app
scenarios.situation: An e-commerce app idles most of the day but gets 20x traffic spikes during flash sales. It currently runs on one oversized VM, 24/7.
scenarios.prompt: What architecture handles this most cost-effectively?
choices: A load balancer with auto-scaling: add instances as traffic rises, remove them as it falls
A single even bigger VM running all the time
Vertical scaling by hand before each sale
Move it back on-premises
scenarios.why: Auto-scaling matches capacity to demand automatically, and the load balancer spreads traffic across the fleet. Paying for peak capacity around the clock wastes money; manual vertical scaling is slow and error-prone under flash-sale pressure.
scenarios.hint: What matches capacity to demand without a human watching?

scenarios.title: Picking the storage tier
scenarios.situation: An app needs storage for two things: millions of user-uploaded images, and a relational database with heavy random reads and writes.
scenarios.prompt: Which pairing is correct?
choices: Object storage for the images; block storage volumes for the database
Block storage for everything
File storage for everything
Archive tape for the database
scenarios.why: Object storage is built for massive numbers of flat, immutable blobs (images, backups) with HTTP access; databases need low-latency block devices that look like local disks. Matching the access pattern to the storage type is a core Cloud+ skill.
scenarios.hint: What storage is built for billions of flat files?

scenarios.title: The deadline migration
scenarios.situation: A legacy app must leave a colo data center before the contract ends in three months. There is no time for a rewrite.
scenarios.prompt: Which migration strategy fits, and what is the trade-off?
choices: Lift-and-shift (rehost) now to meet the deadline, then plan modernization later — it carries tech debt into the cloud
Refactor to cloud-native first, deadline or not
Stay and renegotiate at any cost
Rewrite from scratch in three months
scenarios.why: Rehosting moves the app as-is: fastest, lowest risk to the deadline, but you inherit on-prem architectures (and costs) in the cloud. Refactoring is better long-term but cannot fit the timeline — so rehost now, replatform/refactor in phases.
scenarios.hint: What gets you moved before the contract ends?

scenarios.title: The residency requirement
scenarios.situation: A healthcare company wants cloud elasticity, but regulations require patient records to stay in-country in facilities it controls.
scenarios.prompt: Which deployment model fits?
choices: Hybrid cloud: regulated data on the private side, elastic workloads bursting to public
All-public cloud — regulations are just paperwork
All on-premises — give up elasticity
Ignore the residency rule
scenarios.why: Hybrid keeps sensitive data where the law demands while using public cloud for scale where it is allowed. Data residency and sovereignty requirements are hard constraints that architecture must satisfy, not risks to accept.
scenarios.hint: Where must regulated data physically live?

scenarios.title: The surprise bill
scenarios.situation: The monthly cloud bill doubled. Investigation shows dozens of idle dev VMs running 24/7 and untagged resources nobody claims.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic fix?
choices: Rightsizing, mandatory tagging with ownership, and auto-shutdown schedules for non-production
Pay the bill and hope next month is better
Buy a bigger discount plan and change nothing
Move to another cloud
scenarios.why: Cloud waste is an operational discipline problem: tagging establishes ownership for chargeback, rightsizing matches instances to actual use, and schedules kill idle dev spend. FinOps basics beat provider-hopping every time.
scenarios.hint: What identifies who owns each resource?

scenarios.title: The unreadable web files
scenarios.situation: After a restore, the web server returns 403 Forbidden on every page. The files are owned by the deploy user.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong and what is the fix?
choices: Files are 600 — the web server user cannot read them; set files to 644 and directories to 755
Set everything to 777 so nothing is ever blocked
Change ownership to root
Reinstall the web server
scenarios.why: 600 gives read/write to the owner only; the web server runs as a different user and needs read on files plus read+execute on directories to traverse them. 644/755 is the standard; 777 hands write access to everyone — a vulnerability, not a fix.
scenarios.hint: What does the web server user need — read, write, or both?

scenarios.title: The failed service
scenarios.situation: After a reboot, the application service did not start. The config file was edited yesterday.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct diagnostic sequence?
choices: systemctl status app.service, then journalctl -u app.service to read the failure logs
Reboot again and hope
Reinstall the application
kill -9 the service
scenarios.why: systemctl status shows the state and the most recent log lines; journalctl -u gives the full story, usually a config syntax error from yesterday's edit. Guessing with reinstalls wastes the evidence systemd already collected.
scenarios.hint: Where does systemd keep the service's last words?

scenarios.title: Root filesystem full
scenarios.situation: A Linux host alerts: the root filesystem is at 100%. The application data lives on a separate mounted volume with free space.
scenarios.prompt: How do you find and fix it?
choices: Use du to find the growth (often /var/log), then rotate, compress, or archive — never delete blindly
Run rm -rf /var to clear space fast
Add RAM
Reboot and hope the filesystem recovers
scenarios.why: df identifies the full filesystem, du -sh /* drills into the culprit — typically unrotated logs. Deleting system directories breaks the OS; logrotate plus archival fixes the cause and prevents recurrence.
scenarios.hint: Which command shows where the gigabytes actually are?

scenarios.title: The brute-force noise
scenarios.situation: Auth logs show thousands of SSH password attempts per hour against your public-facing Linux server.
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest mitigation set?
choices: Key-only authentication (disable PasswordAuthentication), plus fail2ban and no direct root login
Just change the SSH port and call it done
Allow root login for convenience
Use longer passwords and keep password auth
scenarios.why: Keys cannot be guessed, so disabling password auth kills brute force entirely; fail2ban adds rate-limiting, and PermitRootLogin no stops the highest-value target. Changing ports is obscurity — it reduces log noise, not risk.
scenarios.hint: What authentication method cannot be guessed?

scenarios.title: The silent cron job
scenarios.situation: A backup script runs perfectly by hand but never runs from cron. There are no errors anywhere obvious.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: Cron's minimal environment — missing PATH or env vars the script relied on from your shell
Cron is broken on this server
The server needs a reboot
Run it manually forever instead
scenarios.why: Cron runs with a sparse environment: no interactive PATH, no aliases, no sourced profiles. Scripts that assume your shell's environment fail silently. Fixes: absolute paths, explicit env vars in the crontab, and logging output to a file.
scenarios.hint: What environment does cron NOT give your script?

scenarios.title: Installing from the wild
scenarios.situation: A blog post says to install a monitoring agent with curl | sudo bash from the author's personal site.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe alternative?
choices: Install from the official distro repository or the vendor's signed repo via apt/dnf, verifying signatures
Pipe the script — the blog has many likes
Download a random tarball and compile as root
Disable GPG checking to make installs faster
scenarios.why: curl|bash executes unaudited code as root from whoever controls that server today. Official repositories provide signed, versioned, updatable packages — the supply-chain-safe path. Convenience is not a security control.
scenarios.hint: Who signed that package — and who controls the download server?

scenarios.title: Four disks, speed plus safety
scenarios.situation: A database server has four identical disks. Requirements: good performance AND survive at least one disk failure.
scenarios.prompt: Which RAID level is the best fit?
choices: RAID 10
RAID 0
RAID 5
JBOD
scenarios.why: RAID 10 is a stripe of mirrors: mirroring survives disk failures (and rebuilds fast), striping delivers performance. RAID 0 has no redundancy, and RAID 5's parity rebuilds on large disks are slow and risky — RAID 10 is the standard answer for performance + redundancy.
scenarios.hint: Which level is a stripe of mirrors?

scenarios.title: The random crashes
scenarios.situation: A server crashes randomly with no useful logs — sometimes kernel panics, sometimes application faults, never the same error twice.
scenarios.prompt: What hardware cause should you suspect, and what is server-grade prevention?
choices: Failing RAM / cosmic-bit flips — use ECC memory, which detects and corrects single-bit errors, and test the DIMMs
The OS needs reinstalling
The PSU is too big
Ignore it; random crashes are normal
scenarios.why: Inconsistent, unlogged crashes are the classic signature of memory errors. ECC RAM corrects single-bit errors in hardware and logs them — which is why servers use it and desktops usually do not. Memtest plus DIMM isolation finds the bad stick.
scenarios.hint: What flips bits silently with no log entry?

scenarios.title: The dead power supply
scenarios.situation: Monitoring alerts: one of two redundant PSUs has failed, but the server is still running.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct action?
choices: Hot-swap the failed PSU now — that is what redundancy is for — and verify the redundancy configuration
Power the server down first to be safe
Ignore it since the server is up
Replace both PSUs
scenarios.why: Redundant hot-swappable PSUs exist so a failure is a maintenance event, not an outage — but redundancy is now gone, so the next failure is fatal. Replace promptly during a planned moment, and confirm the PSUs are on separate circuits.
scenarios.hint: What is the second PSU for?

scenarios.title: The hot aisle
scenarios.situation: Temperature sensors show a steady climb in one rack row over two weeks. Servers there are thermal-throttling.
scenarios.prompt: What do you check first?
choices: Airflow and cooling: HVAC function, blanking panels, hot/cold aisle containment, blocked vents
Install more servers in the row
Open all the rack doors permanently
Ignore it until something shuts down
scenarios.why: Heat problems are airflow problems first: missing blanking panels let hot exhaust recirculate into intakes, defeating the HVAC. Hot/cold aisle discipline plus sealed racks keeps cooling effective; adding load or opening doors makes it worse.
scenarios.hint: Where does the hot exhaust air go?

scenarios.title: POST reports memory errors
scenarios.situation: A server fails to boot, and POST reports memory errors on DIMM B2.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct procedure?
choices: Reseat the DIMMs, then test one at a time to isolate the faulty stick and replace it
Update the BIOS and hope
Reinstall the OS
Ignore POST errors
scenarios.why: POST memory errors localize the fault to a slot or stick. Reseating fixes contact issues; single-stick testing isolates the failure; replace only the bad DIMM. Firmware updates do not fix bad RAM, and the OS is irrelevant before boot.
scenarios.hint: What is the cheapest test you can run first?

scenarios.title: The hung server 200 miles away
scenarios.situation: A branch-office server is completely hung — no SSH, no services. Driving there takes four hours.
scenarios.prompt: What capability resolves this remotely?
choices: Out-of-band management (BMC / iDRAC / iLO) for console access and power control independent of the OS
Wait for it to fix itself
Ask a non-technical employee to pull the plug
Reinstall the OS remotely
scenarios.why: Baseboard management controllers run independently of the host OS: they give KVM console, power cycle, and hardware sensors even when the OS is dead. It is the standard answer for lights-out remote sites — no BMC means a truck roll.
scenarios.hint: What manages the server when the OS is dead?

scenarios.title: Snapshots are not backups
scenarios.situation: An admin proudly reports the VMs are 'backed up' — they take a snapshot of each VM every night and keep them for a month.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this picture?
choices: Snapshots are not backups: they live on the same storage, grow into performance problems, and die with the datastore
Nothing — snapshots are a complete backup strategy
They should take more snapshots
They should delete old snapshots to save space and call it done
scenarios.why: A snapshot is a delta file chained to the base disk on the same storage: lose the datastore and you lose base plus snapshots. Long snapshot chains also degrade performance. Real backups are independent, restorable copies — ideally offsite and tested.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the snapshots when the datastore dies?

scenarios.title: The sluggish VMs
scenarios.situation: VMs on a host are sluggish though the host's CPU graphs look fine. The hypervisor reports high CPU ready time.
scenarios.prompt: What is the cause and fix?
choices: vCPU overprovisioning — VMs are waiting for physical CPU; right-size vCPUs and check contention
Give every VM more vCPUs
Add more RAM to the host
Reboot the host weekly
scenarios.why: CPU ready time measures how long a VM waits for a physical core: over-allocated vCPUs make scheduling harder, not faster. Adding vCPUs to contended hosts worsens it. Right-sizing plus DRS-style balancing restores performance.
scenarios.hint: What does CPU ready time actually measure?

scenarios.title: Fifty microservices
scenarios.situation: A team needs to run fifty small microservices that scale up and down frequently. Full VMs feel heavy and slow to start.
scenarios.prompt: Why are containers the better fit here?
choices: Containers share the host kernel, so they start in milliseconds with far less overhead than full VMs
Containers are just faster VMs with their own kernels
One VM per microservice is simpler
Bare metal for each service
scenarios.why: Containers package the app with its dependencies but share the host OS kernel — no guest OS per instance, no hypervisor boot. That means sub-second starts and dense packing, ideal for elastic microservices. VMs still win where strong isolation or different kernels are needed.
scenarios.hint: What do containers share that VMs do not?

scenarios.title: Patching without downtime
scenarios.situation: A hypervisor host needs firmware patches, but its twenty VMs cannot have downtime.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct procedure?
choices: Live-migrate (vMotion) the running VMs to another host, patch the empty host, then migrate back
Shut everything down for the patch window
Patch the host with VMs running on it
Skip the firmware patches
scenarios.why: Live migration moves running VMs between hosts with no downtime, letting you evacuate a host for maintenance. It requires shared storage and compatible hosts — the standard enterprise maintenance workflow.
scenarios.hint: What moves a running VM without stopping it?

scenarios.title: Choosing the hypervisor
scenarios.situation: You are designing a new virtualization cluster for production workloads needing near-native performance and strong isolation.
scenarios.prompt: Which hypervisor type fits, and why?
choices: Type 1 (bare-metal) — runs directly on hardware with minimal overhead and strong isolation
Type 2 (hosted) — runs on top of a desktop OS
No hypervisor — containers replace everything
Type 2 for production performance
scenarios.why: Type 1 hypervisors (ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM) sit directly on hardware: lower overhead, better isolation, built for data centers. Type 2 (VirtualBox, Workstation) rides on a host OS — fine for labs, wrong for production clusters.
scenarios.hint: What sits directly on the hardware?

scenarios.title: The VM graveyard
scenarios.situation: The cluster has 300 VMs. Nobody can say who owns forty of them, and half have not been powered on in a year.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic fix?
choices: Tagging with ownership, lifecycle policies, and chargeback/showback so orphans get reclaimed
Delete VMs at random
Buy more hosts
Ignore the orphans
scenarios.why: VM sprawl wastes licenses, backup windows, and attack surface. Mandatory tags (owner, purpose, expiry) plus automated reclamation workflows turn sprawl into a managed lifecycle instead of a graveyard.
scenarios.hint: Who owns that VM from 2019?

scenarios.title: Sorting the data zoo
scenarios.situation: A project involves three datasets: transaction records, server log files, and product photos.
scenarios.prompt: How do you classify them?
choices: Transactions are structured (rows/columns); logs are semi-structured; photos are unstructured
Everything is structured data
Everything is big data regardless of form
Classification does not matter
scenarios.why: Structured data fits relational tables; semi-structured (JSON logs) has tags but no fixed schema; unstructured (images, video) has no predefined model. The classification drives storage, tooling, and analysis choices.
scenarios.hint: Which dataset fits neatly in rows and columns?

scenarios.title: Combining the tables
scenarios.situation: You need each customer's name alongside their order totals. Customers live in one table, orders in another.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct approach?
choices: JOIN the tables on the shared customer_id key, then aggregate with GROUP BY
Run two separate queries and merge them by hand in a spreadsheet
Export both tables to CSV and eyeball it
Use SELECT * with no join condition
scenarios.why: A JOIN combines related rows via the key they share; GROUP BY with SUM then rolls orders up per customer. A join without a condition creates a Cartesian product — every customer times every order — which is never what you want.
scenarios.hint: What relates the two tables to each other?
evidence:
customers(customer_id, name)
orders(order_id, customer_id, total)
-- need: name + SUM(total) per customer

scenarios.title: Garbage in
scenarios.situation: Source systems feed your warehouse dirty data: duplicate rows, wrong date formats, nulls in required fields.
scenarios.prompt: Where do you fix it?
choices: In the ETL pipeline: validate, cleanse, and transform before loading into the warehouse
Load it raw and let analysts fix it in every report
Skip validation to load faster
Fix it by hand each morning
scenarios.why: The transform stage exists to enforce quality once, upstream: standardize formats, dedupe, reject or quarantine bad rows. Cleaning downstream means every report reinvents (and disagrees on) the fixes.
scenarios.hint: When is bad data cheapest to catch?

scenarios.title: The duplicated customer
scenarios.situation: Customer addresses are stored in every order row. A customer moves, one row gets updated, and now reports show two addresses.
scenarios.prompt: What database design principle prevents this?
choices: Normalization: store the customer once in a customer table and reference it by ID
Store even more copies for safety
Buy a bigger database
Delete the old rows by hand
scenarios.why: Update anomalies come from duplicated facts: normalization keeps each fact in one place, referenced by key, so a change happens once. Denormalization has performance uses, but it trades away this integrity.
scenarios.hint: What happens when the address changes in only one copy?

scenarios.title: Analytics on customer data
scenarios.situation: Analysts want to study purchasing patterns in production customer data that includes names, emails, and card numbers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct handling?
choices: Mask or anonymize PII, work on the minimum necessary fields, and enforce retention limits
Give analysts raw production data — they are employees
Email CSV extracts around for convenience
No controls needed for internal use
scenarios.why: Analytics rarely needs real identities: masking/anonymization plus least-privilege access preserves utility while limiting breach impact and meeting privacy obligations. Raw PII in spreadsheets is how breaches happen.
scenarios.hint: Does the analyst need real names and card numbers?

scenarios.title: Showing the trend
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants to see monthly revenue over the past two years to judge growth.
scenarios.prompt: Which visualization is appropriate?
choices: A line chart — it shows change over continuous time
A pie chart of all 24 months
A 3D exploding pie chart
A raw data table with no chart
scenarios.why: Line charts encode time on an axis so trends, seasonality, and inflection points are visible at a glance. Pie charts compare parts of a whole at one moment — 24 slices communicate nothing about growth.
scenarios.hint: What shows change across months best?

scenarios.title: The database backup
scenarios.situation: A critical database is backed up nightly to disk on the same server. Restores have never been tested.
scenarios.prompt: What must change to meet a 4-hour RPO?
choices: Follow 3-2-1 with offsite copies, back up at least every 4 hours, and test restores regularly
Keep the single nightly copy — RAID protects it
Back up weekly to save space
Trust that backups work without testing
scenarios.why: RPO is the maximum tolerable data loss: a 4-hour RPO needs backups at least every 4 hours. Same-server copies die with the server (RAID is not backup), and untested restores are unproven — test on a schedule.
scenarios.hint: What does a 4-hour RPO demand of your backup frequency?

scenarios.title: Patch Tuesday for production
scenarios.situation: Security patches are released for your production hypervisors and guest servers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct patching workflow?
choices: Test in staging first, then deploy in a maintenance window with a rollback plan
Patch production directly — speed matters most
Never patch production
Enable auto-patching on everything with no oversight
scenarios.why: Patches fix vulnerabilities but can break workloads: staging catches regressions, windows bound the blast radius, and rollback plans bound the outage. Untested production patching trades one risk for another.
scenarios.hint: Where do bad patches go first?

scenarios.title: Drowning in alerts
scenarios.situation: The monitoring system sends 500 emails a day. Engineers now ignore all of them — including real outages.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Tune thresholds, aggregate related alerts, and tier severities so critical pages are rare and real
Add more checks for coverage
Ignore everything until something breaks
Disable monitoring to stop the noise
scenarios.why: Alert fatigue is a tuning failure: when everything is critical, nothing is. Baselines drive thresholds, aggregation kills storms, and severity tiers protect the paging channel for genuine emergencies.
scenarios.hint: What happens when everything is critical?

scenarios.title: The firewall rule request
scenarios.situation: A developer needs a new firewall rule opened for a production deployment tonight.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct process?
choices: Submit a change request: business justification, risk review, approval, implementation, and verification
Add the rule now, document later
Email the firewall admin after adding it
Freeze all firewall changes forever
scenarios.why: Firewall changes alter the security boundary: they need the same change control as any production change — justification, approval, testing, and a backout plan. 'Temporary' undocumented rules become permanent holes.
scenarios.hint: What stops a temporary rule from becoming permanent?

scenarios.title: Auditing the ruleset
scenarios.situation: You inherit a firewall with 400 rules, many years old, in random order with no comments.
scenarios.prompt: What principles guide the cleanup?
choices: Default-deny, least privilege, remove unused rules, and order specific rules before general ones
Allow all traffic both directions for simplicity
Rule order does not matter
Stop logging to improve performance
scenarios.why: Firewalls evaluate top-down: specific allows/denies must precede general ones, and an explicit deny-all closes the bottom. Stale rules accumulate risk — each unused allow is an unreviewed hole. Document every rule's owner and purpose.
scenarios.hint: What should the last rule in the list be?

scenarios.title: The compromised web server
scenarios.situation: You confirm a public web server is compromised and beaconing out. It also hosts the company's main site.
scenarios.prompt: What are the correct FIRST actions?
choices: Isolate the host from the network, preserve logs and memory for forensics, and invoke the incident response plan
Keep it running to watch the attacker
Wipe and rebuild it immediately
Hide the incident to avoid embarrassment
scenarios.why: Isolation stops spread and exfiltration; preserving volatile evidence (memory, logs) enables forensics and legal action; the IR plan coordinates the rest. Wiping first destroys evidence, and watching an active compromise risks the whole network.
scenarios.hint: What does wiping destroy besides the malware?

lessons.title: CompTIA Infrastructure (Network+/Server+ Track) — Core concepts
concepts: IP addressing is hierarchical: the subnet mask splits every address into network and host portions. Two hosts communicate directly only when they share a network — otherwise traffic goes through the gateway.
Subnet math is powers of two: borrowing n bits creates 2^n subnets with 2^(32-n) - 2 usable hosts each. A /26 carved from a /24 yields four subnets of 62 usable hosts.

Switches versus routers: switches forward within a broadcast domain using MAC tables; routers separate broadcast domains and forward between networks using IP routing tables. VLANs need a router (or layer-3 switch) to talk to each other.
DNS and DHCP are the invisible infrastructure: DHCP automates addressing (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge); DNS translates names. When the internet is 'down' but IPs ping, suspect DNS.

Virtualization abstracts hardware: a type-1 hypervisor runs on bare metal for production servers; type-2 runs atop an OS for labs and desktops. VMs share physical NICs and storage through virtual switches and datastores.

Storage protocols fit workloads: block storage (iSCSI, Fibre Channel) for databases and VM datastores needing raw disks; file storage (SMB, NFS) for shared files; object storage for scale-out unstructured data.

example.code:
ip -brief addr show
ip route show default
example.walkthrough: The first command shows each interface's IP address and mask; the second shows the default gateway. If the address and mask are right but the gateway is missing or wrong, the LAN works and the internet does not.

pitfalls: Common trap: assigning the network or broadcast address to a host — for example .0 or .255 in a /24.
Common trap: confusing a switch with a router — adding another switch never fixes an inter-VLAN routing problem.
Common trap: overlapping subnets on VPN tunnels — identical ranges on both sides break routing.
Common trap: forgetting DNS — 'can't reach the site by name but the IP works' is a DNS problem, not a routing problem.

simulations.title: The disk that filled up
simulations.brief: A VM stops accepting writes: the app logs 'No space left on device', but the dashboard shows the disk at 57%.

steps.symptom: Writes fail with 'No space left', yet the volume shows 57% used.
evidence:
$ df
/dev/sda1  57% /
$ echo test > /tmp/t
bash: /tmp/t: No space left on device
options: Suspect inode exhaustion: check inode usage — a full inode table blocks new files with space to spare
steps.explain: 'No space left' with free blocks means inodes, not bytes: millions of tiny files (often runaway logs or sessions) exhausted the inode table.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: inode table at 100% on /tmp — millions of session files.
options: Clear the stale session files and fix the app to clean up sessions (tmpwatch/cron)
steps.explain: Clear the symptom (stale files) AND the cause (no session cleanup). Disk expansion wouldn't help — inodes, not bytes, were exhausted.

steps.symptom: Cleanup done. Verify the fix holds.
evidence:
$ df -i
/dev/sda1  12% /
$ echo test > /tmp/t && echo OK
OK
options: Confirm writes succeed and inode usage is healthy, and the cleanup job is scheduled
steps.explain: Writes succeeding plus healthy inodes plus a scheduled cleanup is the complete fix — one without the others recurs.

simulations.debrief: 'No space left' with free space means inodes. Clear the files, fix the leak (session cleanup), schedule the prevention. df without -i only tells half the story.

simulations.title: Virtualization stack order
simulations.brief: Restore the order of the virtualization stack from silicon to app.

items: Physical hardware: CPU, RAM, disk
Hypervisor manages the hardware

Guest OS runs on the VM
Application runs on the guest OS

simulations.debrief: Hardware → hypervisor → VM → guest OS → app. Each layer's failure looks different — and gets fixed at its own layer.

simulations.title: Scale up or scale out?
simulations.brief: Choose the scaling strategy for two workloads.

steps.text: A stateful database is slow. It holds 2 TB and can't easily shard. Strategy?

choices.label: Scale up: bigger instance — stateful stores with hard sharding limits scale vertically first
choices.feedback: Right: when the data can't split, grow the box. Sharding a 2 TB store under load is a migration, not a scaling event.

choices.label: Scale out: add 10 replicas
choices.feedback: Replicas of a write-heavy unshardable store multiply the consistency problem, not the capacity.

choices.label: Delete old data
choices.feedback: Deleting production data to fix performance is data loss with extra steps.

steps.text: A stateless API tier is slow at peak. Strategy?

choices.label: Scale out: add instances behind the load balancer — stateless tiers scale horizontally
choices.feedback: Right: stateless means any instance can serve any request — add more of them.

choices.label: Scale up: one giant instance
choices.feedback: One giant instance is a single point of failure with a scaling ceiling.

simulations.debrief: Stateful and hard-to-shard → scale up. Stateless → scale out. The workload's statefulness decides, not the cloud bill.

simulations.title: The backup that never ran
simulations.brief: Backups report 'success' but restores find nothing. The backup config has 2 bugs in 8 lines.

steps.config:
schedule: daily 02:00
source: /data
target: /mnt/backup
retention: 7
verify: false
notify: never
# last restore test: never
# owner: infra-team

issues.description: verify: false — backups are never validated, so silent corruption or empty runs report success.
issues.fix: Enable verification (checksums/test restores) on every run.

issues.description: No restore has ever been tested — an untested backup is a hope, not a recovery plan.
issues.fix: Run scheduled restore drills and record the results.

simulations.debrief: Backups are only real if they're verified and restores are tested. 'Success' without verification is a green lie.

sections.heading: Cloud Architecture

IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — the line moves up the stack with PaaS and SaaS, but IaaS guests are always the customer's job.
Auto-scaling — Auto-scaling matches capacity to demand automatically, and the load balancer spreads traffic across the fleet.
Storage types — object storage is built for massive numbers of flat, immutable blobs (images, backups) with HTTP access; databases need low-latency block devices that look like local disks.
